part: Part IV: The Myth of Sisyphus
title: 11. The Myth of Sisyphus

orig_sentences: The gods had condemned Sisyphus to ceaselessly rolling a rock to the top of a mountain, whence the stone would fall back of its own weight.
They had thought with some reason that there is no more dreadful punishment than futile and hopeless labor.
mod_sentences: The gods had condemned Sisyphus to roll a massive boulder ceaselessly to the top of a mountain, only for the stone to roll back down of its own weight.
They reasoned, not without cause, that there is no punishment more terrible than labor that is entirely futile and hopeless.
pairs.move: Camus opens the myth with the psychology of divine punishment: the ultimate torment is not physical agony, but endless exertion permanently stripped of purpose, progress, or conclusion.

orig_sentences: If one believes Homer, Sisyphus was the wisest and most prudent of mortals.
According to another tradition, however, he was disposed to practice the profession of highwayman.
I see no contradiction in this.
Opinions differ as to the reasons why he became the futile laborer of the underworld.
To begin with, he is accused of a certain levity in regard to the gods.
He stole their secrets.
Ægina, the daughter of Æsopus, was carried off by Jupiter.
The father was shocked by that disappearance and complained to Sisyphus.
He, who knew of the abduction, offered to tell about it on condition that Æsopus would give water to the citadel of Corinth.
To the celestial thunderbolts he preferred the benediction of water.
He was punished for this in the underworld.
Homer tells us also that Sisyphus had put Death in chains.
Pluto could not endure the sight of his deserted, silent empire.
He dispatched the god of war, who liberated Death from the hands of her conqueror.
mod_sentences: If we trust Homer, Sisyphus was the wisest and most prudent of mortals.
According to another tradition, however, he was inclined toward banditry.
I see no contradiction here.
Opinions differ regarding why he was condemned to be the underworld's futile laborer.
To begin with, he was accused of treating the gods with insolent disrespect.
He betrayed their secrets.
Jupiter abducted Aegina, the daughter of the river god Asopus.
Devastated by her disappearance, the father complained to Sisyphus.
Sisyphus, knowing of the abduction, offered to reveal the culprit on one condition: that Asopus provide a freshwater spring to the citadel of Corinth.
He preferred the tangible blessing of water to the fear of celestial thunderbolts.
For this act of defiance, he was sentenced to the underworld.
Homer also recounts that Sisyphus actually put Death herself in chains.
Pluto could not tolerate the sight of his kingdom lying deserted and silent.
He dispatched the god of war, who finally wrestled Death free from the hands of her captor.
pairs.move: Sisyphus's rebellion is rooted in terrestrial solidarity and a visceral passion for life: he chooses water for his mortal city over reverence for Zeus, and chains Death to protect humanity from annihilation.

orig_sentences: It is said also that Sisyphus, being near to death, rashly wanted to test his wife’s love.
He ordered her to cast his unburied body into the middle of the public square.
Sisyphus woke up in the underworld.
And there, annoyed by an obedience so contrary to human love, he obtained from Pluto permission to return to earth in order to chastise his wife.
But when he had seen again the face of this world, enjoyed water and sun, warm stones and the sea, he no longer wanted to go back to the infernal darkness.
Recalls, signs of anger, warnings were of no avail.
Many years more he lived facing the curve of the gulf, the sparkling sea, and the smiles of earth.
A decree of the gods was necessary.
Mercury came and seized the impudent man by the collar and, snatching him from his joys, led him forcibly back to the underworld, where his rock was ready for him.
mod_sentences: It is also said that when Sisyphus lay near death, he rashly resolved to test his wife's devotion.
He ordered her to cast his unburied corpse into the middle of the public square.
Sisyphus awoke in the underworld.
Outraged by an obedience so contrary to genuine human affection, he obtained Pluto's permission to return to earth to punish his wife.
Yet once he beheld the radiant face of this world again—tasting water and sunlight, resting against warm stones, and gazing out at the sea—he refused to return to the infernal darkness.
Divine summonses, furious outbursts, and solemn warnings proved entirely useless.
For many years he lived on, facing the curve of the bay, the glittering water, and the warmth of the earth.
In the end, an absolute decree from Olympus became necessary.
Mercury arrived, seized the insolent man by the collar, snatched him away from his pleasures, and dragged him forcibly back to the underworld, where his boulder was waiting.
pairs.move: The second defiance: Tasting the sensory world once more, Sisyphus rejects eternity and divine authority. His revolt is purely immanent—he chooses the warmth of the sun and sea over any promised transcendent afterlife.

orig_sentences: You have already grasped that Sisyphus is the absurd hero.
He is, as much through his passions as through his torture.
His scorn of the gods, his hatred of death, and his passion for life won him that unspeakable penalty in which the whole being is exerted toward accomplishing nothing.
This is the price that must be paid for the passions of this earth.
Nothing is told us about Sisyphus in the underworld.
Myths are made for the imagination to breathe life into them.

As for this myth, one sees merely the whole effort of a body straining to raise the huge stone, to roll it and push it up a slope a hundred times over; one sees the face screwed up, the cheek tight against the stone, the shoulder bracing the claycovered mass, the foot wedging it, the fresh start with arms outstretched, the wholly human security of two earth-clotted hands.
At the very end of his long effort measured by skyless space and time without depth, the purpose is achieved.
Then Sisyphus watches the stone rush down in a few moments toward that lower world whence he will have to push it up again toward the summit.
He goes back down to the plain.
mod_sentences: It is already obvious why Sisyphus is the archetype of the absurd hero.
He embodies it as much through his earthly passions as through his punishment.
His defiance toward the gods, his hatred of death, and his ferocious passion for life earned him that unspeakable penalty: an entire existence spent straining toward absolute futility.
This is the price demanded for loving the things of this earth.
The ancient myths tell us almost nothing about his daily existence in the underworld.
Yet myths exist precisely for the imagination to animate them.

In this myth, what we see is the sheer physical effort of a body straining to lift the colossal stone, rolling it and pushing it up a slope hundreds of times: the contorted face, the cheek pressed hard against the rock, the shoulder wedged under the clay-caked mass, the foot bracing against the earth, the repeated thrust with outstretched arms, and the raw, vulnerable humanity of two mud-stained hands.
At the conclusion of this long exertion—measured in skyless space and time without depth—the summit is reached.
Then Sisyphus watches the boulder tumble down in a matter of moments into the valley below, from where he will have to push it upward all over again.
He turns and walks back down to the plain.
pairs.move: Sisyphus as visceral archetype. Camus de-mythologizes the fable by grounding it in muscular, tactile reality: cheek against stone, mud-caked hands, and repetitive physical strain, transforming metaphysical punishment into concrete human labor.

orig_sentences: It is during that return, that pause, that Sisyphus interests me.
A face that toils so close to stones is already stone itself!
I see that man going back down with a heavy yet measured step toward the torment of which he will never know the end.
That hour like a breathing-space which returns as surely as his suffering, that is the hour of consciousness.
At each of those moments when he leaves the heights and gradually sinks toward the lairs of the gods, he is superior to his fate.
He is stronger than his rock.
mod_sentences: It is precisely during that return, during that brief pause, that Sisyphus commands my attention.
A face that labors in such brutal proximity to stone becomes stone itself.
I envision that man descending with a heavy yet rhythmic stride toward an agony that will never end.
That interval—a breathing space that returns as reliably as his suffering—is the hour of consciousness.
At each of those moments when he departs the summit and descends toward the underworld of the gods, he rises superior to his fate.
He is stronger than the rock he must roll.
pairs.move: The pause of consciousness. The descent down the mountain is the philosophical center of the essay. In this brief breathing space, free from the physical weight of the stone, lucid awareness turns a slave of fate into its master.

orig_sentences: If this myth is tragic, that is because its hero is conscious.
Where would his torture be, indeed, if at every step the hope of succeeding upheld him?
The workman of today works every day in his life at the same tasks, and this fate is no less absurd.
But it is tragic only at the rare moments when it becomes conscious.
Sisyphus, proletarian of the gods, powerless and rebellious, knows the whole extent of his wretched condition: it is what he thinks of during his descent.
The lucidity that was to constitute his torture at the same time crowns his victory.
There is no fate that cannot be surmounted by scorn.
mod_sentences: If this myth is genuinely tragic, it is solely because its hero is conscious.
Where would the torture be, after all, if at every step he were sustained by the illusion of eventual success?
The modern worker labors every day of his life at identical tasks, and his condition is no less absurd.
Yet that existence becomes tragic only in those rare moments when he awakens to full consciousness.
Sisyphus, the proletarian of the gods, powerless yet defiant, grasps the entire expanse of his wretched condition; that is precisely what occupies his mind during the descent.
The radical clarity meant to constitute his torment becomes the very instrument of his triumph.
There is no destiny that cannot be overcome by defiant contempt.
pairs.move: The proletarian analogy and the power of scorn. Modern routine is identical to Sisyphus's labor; both are absurd. Lucidity is a double-edged sword: it makes suffering tragic, but conscious contempt disarms the gods' victory.

orig_sentences: If the descent is thus sometimes performed in sorrow, it can also take place in joy.
This word is not too much.
Again I fancy Sisyphus returning toward his rock, and the sorrow was in the beginning.

When the images of earth cling too tightly to memory, when the call of happiness becomes too insistent, it happens that melancholy rises in man’s heart: this is the rock’s victory, this is the rock itself.
The boundless grief is too heavy to bear.
These are our nights of Gethsemane.
But crushing truths perish from being acknowledged.
Thus, Œdipus at the outset obeys fate without knowing it.
But from the moment he knows, his tragedy begins.
Yet at the same moment, blind and desperate, he realizes that the only bond linking him to the world is the cool hand of a girl.
Then a tremendous remark rings out: “Despite so many ordeals, my advanced age and the nobility of my soul make me conclude that all is well.”
Sophocles’ Œdipus, like Dostoevsky’s Kirilov, thus gives the recipe for the absurd victory.
Ancient wisdom confirms modern heroism.
mod_sentences: While this descent is sometimes undertaken in sorrow, it can equally occur in joy.
That word is by no means an exaggeration.
Once more I picture Sisyphus walking down toward his rock; the sorrow belonged only to the beginning.

When memories of the earth cling too stubbornly to the mind, when the longing for past happiness becomes overwhelming, melancholy floods the human heart: this is the rock's true victory; this is the rock itself.
That boundless grief feels impossible to bear.
These are our personal nights of Gethsemane.
Yet crushing truths lose their power the moment they are lucidly acknowledged.
At the outset, Oedipus blindly obeys a fate he does not recognize.
The moment he learns the truth, his tragedy begins.
Yet at that exact instant, blind and desperate, he realizes that his sole anchor to existence is the cool hand of a young girl.
Then a magnificent declaration rings out: “Despite all my ordeals, my old age and the nobility of my soul compel me to conclude that all is well.”
Sophocles' Oedipus, like Dostoevsky's Kirillov, provides the exact formula for the absurd triumph.
Ancient tragic wisdom validates modern existential courage.
pairs.move: Confronting crushing truth destroys its dominion. Melancholy stems from clinging to false hopes or nostalgic regrets. Oedipus's heroic affirmation (“all is well”) demonstrates that embracing tragedy without illusion transforms despair into sovereign peace.

orig_sentences: One does not discover the absurd without being tempted to write a manual of happiness.
“What! by such narrow ways—?”
There is but one world, however.
Happiness and the absurd are two sons of the same earth.
They are inseparable.
It would be a mistake to say that happiness necessarily springs from the absurd discovery.
It happens as well that the feeling of the absurd springs from happiness.
“I conclude that all is well,” says Œdipus, and that remark is sacred.
It echoes in the wild and limited universe of man.
It teaches that all is not, has not been, exhausted.
It drives out of this world a god who had come into it with dissatisfaction and a preference for futile sufferings.
It makes of fate a human matter, which must be settled among men.
mod_sentences: One cannot discover the absurd without feeling the temptation to write a manual of happiness.
“What! Along such a narrow and unforgiving path?”
Yet there is only one real world.
Happiness and the absurd are twin children of the same earth.
They are entirely inseparable.
It would be an error to claim that happiness arises automatically from realizing the absurd.
Just as often, the sudden intuition of the absurd erupts directly from profound happiness.
“I conclude that all is well,” Oedipus declares, and that statement is sacred.
It reverberates across the wild, bounded horizon of human life.
It teaches that reality is not, and never has been, exhausted.
That single affirmation expels from this world any god who arrived bearing grievances and an appetite for futile suffering.
It restores destiny entirely to human hands, as a matter to be settled strictly among men.
pairs.move: Reclaiming destiny from the divine. The Absurd does not extinguish joy; it births it. By declaring “all is well,” humanity banishes the concept of divine punishment and reclaims existence as an entirely secular, mortal affair.

orig_sentences: All Sisyphus’ silent joy is contained therein.
His fate belongs to him.
His rock is his thing.
Likewise, the absurd man, when he contemplates his torment, silences all the idols.
In the universe suddenly restored to its silence, the myriad wondering little voices of the earth rise up.
Unconscious, secret calls, invitations from all the faces, they are the necessary reverse and price of victory.
There is no sun without shadow, and it is essential to know the night.
The absurd man says yes and his effort will henceforth be unceasing.
If there is a personal fate, there is no higher destiny, or at least there is but one which he concludes is inevitable and despicable.
For the rest, he knows himself to be the master of his days.

At that subtle moment when man glances backward over his life, Sisyphus returning toward his rock, in that slight pivoting he contemplates that series of unrelated actions which becomes his fate, created by him, combined under his memory’s eye and soon sealed by his death.
Thus, convinced of the wholly human origin of all that is human, a blind man eager to see who knows that the night has no end, he is still on the go.
The rock is still rolling.
mod_sentences: The entirety of Sisyphus's silent joy is contained right here.
His fate belongs strictly to him.
His rock is his own domain.
Similarly, when the absurd person looks upon his struggle, he silences every metaphysical idol.
In a universe suddenly returned to its majestic silence, thousands of quiet, marveling voices rise up from the earth.
Unconscious whispers, secret gestures, invitations from countless human faces—these are the necessary counterpart and the price of his triumph.
There is no sunlight without shadow, and one must intimately know the night.
The absurd person says yes to life, and his commitment becomes relentless.
If an individual destiny exists, there is no transcendent Providence governing it—or at most, only a blind mechanism that he recognizes as inevitable and regards with contempt.
Beyond that, he knows he is the sole master of his days.

In that decisive instant when a person casts a backward glance across life—as Sisyphus pivots toward his rock—he surveys that succession of unconnected actions that has coalesced into his destiny, shaped by his own choices, bound together by memory, and soon to be sealed by his death.
Convinced of the purely human origin of everything human—like a blind man who aches to see yet knows the darkness is infinite—he moves forward.
The rock is rolling still.
pairs.move: Total existential autonomy. In silencing the idols, man inherits the silent world. Sisyphus's backward glance affirms that life is an unscripted series of human choices, unified only by personal consciousness and mortal finality.

orig_sentences: I leave Sisyphus at the foot of the mountain!
One always finds one’s burden again.
But Sisyphus teaches the higher fidelity that negates the gods and raises rocks.
He too concludes that all is well.
This universe henceforth without a master seems to him neither sterile nor futile.
Each atom of that stone, each mineral flake of that night-filled mountain, in itself forms a world.
The struggle itself toward the heights is enough to fill a man’s heart.
One must imagine Sisyphus happy.
mod_sentences: I leave Sisyphus at the foot of the mountain.
A person will always return to his burden.
Yet Sisyphus teaches that higher fidelity which repudiates the gods and hoists colossal stones.
He, too, concludes that all is well.
This universe, freed forever from any celestial master, appears to him neither sterile nor meaningless.
Every single atom of that stone, every mineral splinter of that dark mountain, constitutes a complete cosmos in itself.
The struggle toward the heights is itself enough to fill a human heart.
One must imagine Sisyphus happy.
pairs.move: The climactic apotheosis. Life requires no transcendent justification to be profoundly lived; the lucid, relentless exertion against gravity and mortality is its own ultimate reward. Heroic defiance transforms pointless labor into absolute joy.
